igneous.cooling-rate.text: Magma that cools slowly underground grows big crystals. Lava that cools fast at the surface has tiny crystals or none.
igneous.cooling-rate.fieldNote: Slow cooling = big crystals. Fast cooling = tiny or none.

pumice.gas-bubbles.text: Pumice is frothy lava that cooled fast. The holes are gas bubbles that got trapped. It is often light enough to float on water.
pumice.gas-bubbles.fieldNote: Pumice: full of gas-bubble holes, often floats.

obsidian.volcanic-glass.text: Obsidian is volcanic glass. The lava cooled so fast that no crystals had time to grow at all.

basalt.lava-rock.text: Basalt is the most common volcanic rock on Earth. It forms when runny lava cools quickly. Most of Iceland is made of it.
basalt.lava-rock.fieldNote: Basalt: dark lava rock. Most of Iceland is made of it.

map.grid-references.text: A grid reference names one square on a map: the letter across first, then the number down.
map.grid-references.fieldNote: Grid reference: letter across, then number down.

map.compass-north.text: A compass needle points north. Most maps are drawn with north at the top, so you can turn the map to match the ground.
map.compass-north.fieldNote: Compass points north. Maps put north at the top.

iceland.fish-drying.text: In Iceland, fish such as cod and haddock are dried outdoors on wooden racks by wind and cold air. Dried fish (harðfiskur) is a common snack, often eaten with butter.
iceland.fish-drying.fieldNote: Fish is dried on racks by wind. Eaten with butter.
iceland.fish-drying.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Har%C3%B0fiskur (suggested; check against an Icelandic food source)

iceland.fish-export.text: Fish and other sea products are one of Iceland's biggest exports.
iceland.fish-export.fieldNote: Fish is one of Iceland's biggest exports.

iceland.geothermal-heating.text: About nine in ten homes in Iceland are heated with hot water from underground (geothermal heating).
iceland.geothermal-heating.fieldNote: ~9 in 10 Icelandic homes use geothermal heat.
iceland.geothermal-heating.source: https://nea.is/geothermal/ (National Energy Authority of Iceland, suggested)

iceland.sulphur-water.text: In many parts of Iceland the hot tap water comes straight from geothermal sources and can smell of sulphur, like eggs. Cold tap water is ordinary spring or ground water.
iceland.sulphur-water.fieldNote: Hot tap water can smell of sulphur. Cold does not.
iceland.sulphur-water.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geothermal_power_in_Iceland (suggested; check with Veitur, the Reykjavík utility)

iceland.geothermal-bread.text: Some Icelanders bake dark rye bread (rúgbrauð) by burying it in hot geothermal ground for about a day.
iceland.geothermal-bread.fieldNote: Rye bread can be baked slowly in hot ground.

iceland.sheep-rettir.text: Icelandic sheep graze freely in the hills and highlands all summer. In September farmers gather them and sort them in stone pens. This round-up is called réttir.
iceland.sheep-rettir.fieldNote: Sheep roam free in summer. Gathered in Sept (réttir).

iceland.christmas-eve.text: In Iceland the main Christmas celebration is on the evening of 24 December, and many people go to church that evening.
iceland.christmas-eve.fieldNote: Christmas is celebrated on the evening of Dec 24.

plates.divergent-iceland.text: Iceland sits on the boundary where the North American and Eurasian plates move apart, about 2 cm a year. The rift at Þingvellir is that boundary at the surface.
plates.divergent-iceland.fieldNote: Two plates pull apart under Iceland, ~2 cm a year.

geyser.how.text: A geyser is a hot spring that erupts. Water deep underground is heated by hot rock until it boils and blasts the water above it into the air.
geyser.how.fieldNote: Geyser: underground water boils and blasts upward.

basalt.columns.text: When a thick flow of basalt lava cools slowly, it shrinks and cracks into tall columns, often with six sides.
basalt.columns.fieldNote: Cooling lava shrinks and cracks into six-sided columns.

glacier.meltwater-rivers.text: Glaciers are rivers of ice that move slowly downhill. Their meltwater feeds many of Iceland's rivers and waterfalls.
glacier.meltwater-rivers.fieldNote: Glaciers melt into rivers; rivers make the waterfalls.

beach.black-sand.text: Iceland's black beaches are made of basalt broken down by the sea and by glacier floods, not of pale quartz sand like most beaches.
